newsitem.title: FRANCE: C.Lyonnais may need better solvency ratio - analysts.
newsitem.headline: C.Lyonnais may need better solvency ratio - analysts.

text.p: State-owned Credit Lyonnais might need a better Cooke ratio than the 5.5 percent it had said it needed to be privatised, banking analysts quoted the bank's chairman Jean Peyrelevade as saying on Friday.
That could mean an even bigger capital injection than the eight to nine billion francs suggested by the bank on Thursday.

One analyst quoted him as saying a 5.5 percent ratio would be "a little tight" and that 6.0 or 6.5 percent might be needed. But a bank spokesman said Peyrelevade had only been conjecturing about what ratio might be needed under different privatisation scenarios.
Banking analysts underlined that it was difficult to calculate how much the bank would need to be recapitalised by as much would depend on the asset disposals it made.
The bank has said it plans to dispose of many foreign assets ahead of privatisation.
"We could be talking ten billion francs, 15 billion francs," said one. "It's a triple question mark question," said another.
The French government said last week it planned to mount a third bailout of the bank to ready it for privatisation that would be carried out as swiftly as possible.
But it said it wanted to wait for the announcement of the bank's first half figures on Thursday before saying how much money it might inject into the bank.

The bank reported a 67 million franc half-year profit on Thursday, helped by a 3.9 billion franc emergency rescue package package. The package remedied what turned out to be the overly harsh terms of last year's state salvage that would have driven the bank into the red.
The results showed an improvement across the board except for France where operating profits slumped sharply.

But analysts were in the main optimistic the bank could turn around its outlook in France. Banking analyst Sami Gotrane of brokerage EIFB noted that the bank's plan to cut 5,000 jobs from its payroll had yet to take effect which would cut its costs.
"They have the capacity to bring about the recovery of their French activities," he said. "They have a very good network."
But analysts were doubtful about the government's aim of a rapid privatisation, saying the bank had told them it was more likely to take until mid-1998.
